title: The Lantern of the Cape Route
premise: In 1890s Cape Route, a fog-bound port town built on pearl money and buried ledgers, Vesper Blackwood has survived his indenture to the Halloway Trading Company by being useful and unremarkable. When an infant is abandoned at the company door with a note ordering him to forget the face, Vesper recognizes the child as kin to a diver lost in a staged 'accident'—one of many the company has written out of existence. Pulling threads through drowned witnesses, bribed coroners, and a ledger hidden inside the old lighthouse, Vesper assembles proof of the company's crimes while its owners close ranks around him. In the end he smuggles the testimony aboard a departing mail steamer and into the hands of a colonial commission, trading his own freedom—and nearly his life—to make the record permanent before the victors' historians can bleach it clean.
about_author: R. M. Villalobos is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing shipping manifests and indenture records from colonial port towns. Their fiction draws on the marginalia of those documents—the names struck through, the deaths logged as weather.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Hands
chapters.summary: Vesper Blackwood, nineteen and three years from earning out his indenture, works the Halloway Trading Company's counting floor, invisible by design. Through his eyes we learn the town's economy of pearls, debt, and silence. Emotional beat: wary contentment—the safety of being overlooked.

chapters.title: A Bundle at the Door
chapters.summary: During a storm, a crying bundle appears on the company's step with a note: 'Forget the face.' The night clerk orders Vesper to take it to the foundling house and say nothing. He glimpses a birthmark matching one he's seen before—on a dead diver's sister. Beat: dread cracking open routine.

chapters.title: The Drowned Ledger
chapters.summary: Vesper quietly checks the company's casualty rolls and finds diver Elias Marr recorded as 'lost to squall'—though that week's weather log shows calm seas. His POV alternates with a brief interlude from the foundling house matron, who notices the baby's fine clothes. Beat: first cold certainty.

chapters.title: Rules of the Indentured
chapters.summary: Vesper's mentor, the aging clerk Bram Tull, warns him off: questions sank better men. Flashback reveals how Vesper's own father, a diver, died indebted to Halloway. Beat: fear wrestling with inherited grief; Vesper chooses caution—but keeps the note.

chapters.title: The Widow Marr
chapters.summary: Vesper visits Sera Marr, Elias's widow, posing as a clerk verifying pension claims. She knows more than she says and recognizes the baby's swaddling cloth as her sister-in-law's needlework. Beat: two cautious people circling a shared wound, deciding to trust.

chapters.title: Mr. Halloway's Smile
chapters.summary: Company heir Augustin Halloway takes sudden, courteous interest in Vesper—a promotion offer that is really a leash. A second 'accident' claim crosses the desk the same day. Beat: the trap of favor; Vesper accepts the promotion to gain access to sealed files.

chapters.title: What the Tide Keeps
chapters.summary: Sera introduces Vesper to the divers' beach community, where memory survives in songs naming men the ledgers omit. An old diver describes the wreck site where Elias actually died. Beat: communal grief as counter-archive; Vesper begins writing names in a hidden notebook.

chapters.title: The Coroner's Convenient Pen
chapters.summary: Vesper courts drunken ex-coroner Pell, who confesses he signed death certificates dictated by the company. Pell agrees to testify—then sobers and panics. Beat: hope curdling into fragility; the cost of witnesses.

chapters.title: Fire at the Annex
chapters.summary: The records annex burns overnight; the 1888–89 casualty files are ash. Augustin expresses sympathy while watching Vesper too closely. Matron Odile, POV interlude, hides the baby during a visit from company men asking after 'the foundling.' Beat: escalation—the company erases faster than Vesper can record.

chapters.title: Bram's Confession
chapters.summary: Dying Bram admits he falsified entries for thirty years under threat, and gives Vesper a key to a deposit box holding his private duplicate ledger. Beat: the mentor's shame passed down like an inheritance; forgiveness without absolution.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse Room
chapters.summary: The deposit box leads to the decommissioned lighthouse, where a former keeper—company blackmailer turned hermit—stashed corroborating manifests. Vesper finds the pattern: every 'lost' diver was insured against the company. Beat: awe and horror; the scale revealed.

chapters.title: A Name for the Child
chapters.summary: Sera takes the baby in openly, defying the company's quiet campaign of intimidation. Vesper, growing attached, confronts that the child is bait meant to draw out whoever kept the note. Beat: tenderness weaponized; resolve hardening into risk.

chapters.title: Pell Floats In
chapters.summary: Coroner Pell is pulled from the harbor, ruled accidental drowning. Vesper realizes his inquiries are being tracked through the promotion he accepted. Beat: guilt and terror; every ally is now evidence against them.

chapters.title: The Commission Arrives
chapters.summary: A colonial inquiry into port labor conditions docks for eleven days only. Vesper sees the window: get sworn testimony on record before the company's lawyers bury it. Beat: hope with a deadline; the race structure locks in.

chapters.title: Buying Silence
chapters.summary: Halloway offers Vesper full emancipation, passage abroad, and a stipend—for the notebook and the key. Vesper stalls, learning the commissioners have already dined with Augustin. Beat: temptation priced honestly; Veper understands justice must be seized, not granted.

chapters.title: Night Copyists
chapters.summary: Sera, the matron, and beach divers help Vesper copy the lighthouse manifests before the company can seize them. A watchman is bribed, nearly betrayed. Beat: solidarity forged in lamplight; the archive becomes a collective act.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Price
chapters.summary: Company men ransack the lighthouse; the old keeper dies defending it, leaving Vesper the final page naming Augustin's father as architect of the scheme. Beat: martyrdom and fury; Vesper stops calculating and commits.

chapters.title: Sworn and Sealed
chapters.summary: Vesper walks into the commission's temporary chambers and requests to be heard as 'a witness to the record,' presenting duplicates, Bram's ledger, and the keeper's page. Sera testifies about Elias. Beat: climax begins—voice against institution.

chapters.title: Halloway's Counterstroke
chapters.summary: Augustin produces Vesper's forged embezzlement file and demands his arrest mid-hearing. The commissioners waver until Matron Odile arrives with the baby and the original note—physical proof predating the forgery. Beat: climax peak; truth narrowly outsprinting narrative control.

chapters.title: The Steamer's Wake
chapters.summary: Certified copies leave aboard the mail steamer under diplomatic seal; the originals stay hidden with the divers. Augustin is arrested but the family's lawyers circle. Vesper, exposed and expendable, must flee or face retribution. Beat: victory shadowed by cost.

chapters.title: Emancipation Papers
chapters.summary: The commission voids Vesper's indenture as part of interim findings—freedom arriving not as gift but as consequence of testimony. He chooses to stay in Cape Route rather than run. Beat: reclaiming home; survival redefined as presence, not invisibility.

chapters.title: The Lantern Rekindled
chapters.summary: A year later, the lighthouse relit as a public records house, Vesper teaches clerks to read ledgers skeptically. Sera and the child—named Elias—visit the shore where songs now carry verified names. Final beat: memory institutionalized; the record holds because ordinary people kept it.
